roadmap.title: Example: Learn Git fundamentals
roadmap.description: A small sample roadmap that shows every feature. Explore, edit or delete it.
roadmap.overview:
## Goal
Be comfortable using Git day to day: commit deliberately, branch and merge, and collaborate through pull requests.

## Context for agents
The learner can use a terminal and has written small programs. Keep explanations practical with runnable commands.

## What this sample shows
- Main path down the left, sub-checkpoints to the right
- Prerequisites (dashed arrows) and an **optional** branch (Rebase)
- Approved vs. draft content, statuses, and the understanding check
- Notes with checklists and code, resources with a video timestamp

checkpoints.summary: What problem Git solves and the mental model of snapshots.
checkpoints.completion: Explain to a friend why "final_v2_really_final.doc" is a version-control problem.

sections.objectives:
- Describe what a repository, a commit and a snapshot are.
- Contrast centralised and distributed version control.
sections.content:
Git records **snapshots** of a project over time. Each snapshot (a *commit*) knows its parent, so history forms a chain you can inspect, compare and return to.

Because every clone holds the full history, Git is *distributed*: you can commit offline and share later.
sections.known: I have used Google Docs version history, which is similar for single files.
sections.notes:
The key shift for me: Git stores **snapshots**, not lists of edits.

- [x] Read the Pro Git intro
- [x] Watch one overview video
sections.takeaways:
- A commit = snapshot + message + parent pointer.
- Every clone is a full backup.
sections.ownWords: Git is a time machine for a folder: I take labelled photos of the whole folder and can go back to any photo.

sections.content:
```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```
sections.evidence: Ran `git config --list` and saw my name and email.

checkpoints.completion: Make five meaningful commits in a practice repo and find any change with `git log -p`.

sections.objectives:
- Use the staging area to build focused commits.
- Read history with `log` and `diff`.
- Undo mistakes without losing work.
sections.content: A commit is built in two steps: **stage** what you want (`git add`), then **commit** it with a message. Small, focused commits make history readable.
sections.notes: Still confusing: when is `git restore` vs `git reset` the right tool?
sections.questions: - What happens to staged changes if I switch branches?

checkpoints.title: Commits and history

checkpoints.summary: Choose exactly what goes into the next commit.

sections.content:
Files move between three areas: **working tree → staging area (index) → repository**.

```bash
git status        # what changed
git add file.txt  # stage one file
git add -p        # stage hunk by hunk
git commit -m "Explain why, not what"
```
sections.ownWords: Staging is a shopping basket: I put in only what belongs in this commit, then pay (commit).
sections.takeaways: - `git add -p` is the best habit for focused commits.

checkpoints.title: The staging area

checkpoints.summary: Find when and why something changed.

resources.title: Pro Git: Viewing the commit history

sections.content:
```bash
git log --oneline --graph --all
git log -p -- path/to/file
git diff            # unstaged changes
git diff --staged   # what will be committed
```
sections.practice:
1. In a practice repo, make three commits to one file.
2. Use `git log -p` to find the commit that introduced a specific line.

checkpoints.title: Reading history: log and diff

checkpoints.summary: Discard, unstage, amend and revert without losing work.

sections.content:
| Situation | Command |
|---|---|
| Discard unstaged edits | `git restore file` |
| Unstage | `git restore --staged file` |
| Fix last commit message | `git commit --amend` |
| Undo a pushed commit | `git revert <sha>` |
